title: Quantization technical review - Cypher AI
summary: Redwood SE walked Cypher AI team through INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs for their 7B/13B workloads. Discussed accuracy regressions observed in GPTQ vs AWQ, batching and KV cache effects on latency, and on-prem VPC constraints. Agreed next steps to run AWQ and GPTQ benchmarks on Cypher's 7B with 512 and 2048 contexts and share detailed numbers and config. Security docs and SLO targets to be sent.

KV cache behavior and prefix caching
batching policies and latency vs throughput
VPC/on-prem deployment constraints and driver/kernel support

Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-03-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Lena Park (CTO, Cypher AI), Omar Singh (ML Eng), Priya Nair (Infra)

Summary: 
(automated) Short summary above.

--- Transcript (timestamps approx every 30-60s, auto-transcript with occasional errors) ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Diego, our inference SE. How's it going, Lena?
[00:06] Lena: Good, thanks. We wanted to dig into quantization specifics, we saw some accuracy drop on GPTQ in our internal runs and want to understand tradeoffs and options like AWQ or FP8.
[00:15] Diego: Absolutely. We'll cover INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ — tradeoffs across quality/regression, perf, memory. Also we'll discuss batching, KV cache interactions, and your VPC/on-prem constraints.
[00:28] Omar: Quick note — our main production model is a 7B gen model (forked from Llama variant) and a smaller 3B for low-latency routes. We'll likely test 13B for higher accuracy too. Our target P95 latency is 120ms token for interactive, and throughput targets for batch scoring around 4000 tokens/s on dedicated nodes.
[00:45] Diego: Got it. For 7B specifically, AWQ and GPTQ both give big memory wins vs fp16. In our recent tests AWQ tends to be ~5-10% lower perplexity degradation versus GPTQ on certain tasks, but results vary by model and calibration set. GPTQ sometimes introduces visible regressions on instruction-following prompts.
[01:05] Maya: note — transcription may say GTPQ sometimes, ignore that.
[01:09] Lena: We've observed that — some prompts produce hallucinations more often after GPTQ. Curious about why.
[01:15] Diego: Two main reasons: (1) per-layer sensitivity — GPTQ can clip quant errors into critical heads, (2) calibration/data used during quantization. AWQ's approach (group-wise adaptive weight quant) preserves higher-fidelity for outlier weights, so it maps better for instruction-following. But AWQ can be slightly slower at inference than optimized GPTQ kernels if the runtime doesn't have AWQ-specific kernels.
[01:40] Omar: How about INT8 vs FP8? Our infra team was asking about FP8 being future-looking.
[01:44] Diego: FP8 (e4m3/e5m2 styles) can keep more dynamic range than INT8, leading to fewer regressions — but FP8 support is spotty across runtimes and GPU drivers. INT8 with symmetric quant and per-channel scales is more widely supported now, and Redwood has production paths for INT8 (including GPTQ-derived and QAT). For FP8 you'd need hardware and kernel support (some NVIDIA A100/A200 changes and newer drivers).
[02:05] Priya: We're on A100 40GB and a mix of A200s in the staging cluster — driver 535.x. Will that be okay?
[02:13] Diego: A100 is fine, A200 should support FP8 with the right driver; 535.x likely supports some FP8 features but we'd validate. For on-prem we check CUDA + cuBLAS and cuDNN versions; Redwood's private runtime has fallbacks to INT8/GPTQ/AWQ if FP8 not available.
[02:32] Omar: On latency tradeoffs, how does KV cache affect quantized models? We saw increased token latency after applying quantization in our microbenchmarks.
[02:40] Diego: Quantization affects matrix multiply precision and memory layout. Two effects on KV cache: (1) cache size reduced with quantization, so memory pressure decreases which sometimes speeds up cache reads; (2) but if the runtime needs extra dequant+requant steps on the fly, you can see added per-token overhead. Redwood runtime uses fused dequant kernels and keeps KV in native quantized buffers when possible to avoid conversions — reduces per-token overhead. Still, AWQ's grouping may require an extra dequant op depending on kernelization.
[03:10] Lena: So in practice, do we expect +5ms or +20ms token latency?
[03:14] Diego: On 7B with optimized kernels and prefix caching, we typically see token latency within +1-8ms versus fp16 when using our INT8 path; GPTQ without optimized kernels could be +10-25ms. AWQ tends to be in the +3-12ms range depending on kernel support. These are ballpark numbers.
[03:33] Omar: That's useful. Our P95 requirement of 120ms should still be okay for interactive. But throughput for batch scoring — will quantization help?
[03:40] Diego: Yes, quantization usually increases throughput because of smaller memory bandwidth and better cache residency. With 7B on a single A100, INT8/AWQ can double tokens/s for throughput workloads versus fp16 in many scenarios, especially when using larger batch sizes. But the batching policy interacts with latency — bigger batches mean higher throughput but increased tail latency.
[04:00] Priya: About batching — we currently have a shared dedicated pool, can Redwood's router do per-route batching policies?
[04:06] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports per-route batching and dynamic batching thresholds. You can set max_batch_size, max_wait_ms, and also autoscale pool size to keep latency within SLOs. We also have prefix-aware batching to avoid batching across different prefixes that would reduce caching efficiency.
[04:23] Omar: We noticed some weird perf when we had many small prefix variations — KV cache hit rate dropped and throughput tanked.
[04:29] Diego: That's expected. If prefix entropy is high, caching effectiveness drops. We recommend canonicalizing prompts where possible and using prefix templates; also consider longer-lived cached prefixes for interactive flows to amortize overhead.
[04:45] Lena: On accuracy regressions: any mitigation besides retraining or using fp16? Calibration datasets?
[04:51] Diego: Calibration matters a lot. For GPTQ you need a representative calibration set; small mismatches can cause regressions. AWQ typically needs less aggressive calibration and is more robust to outliers. Additional techniques: per-channel clipping, bias correction, and small fine-tuning/QAT passes on critical layers. Also model surgery — keep first and last n layers in fp16 (mixed quant) reduces most regressions with moderate memory cost.
[05:20] Omar: Can Redwood's pipeline do mixed-precision automatically?
[05:23] Diego: We provide quantization profiles and an automated optimizer that suggests mixed precision layers based on eval metric delta. It can produce a profile like: layers [0-3] fp16, [4-28] int8/awq, last 2 layers fp16. We can also run delta-evals on your eval set and recommend a profile.
[05:40] Maya: quick aside — transcript may say 'KV cachen' or similar, ignore minor typos.
[05:45] Priya: For on-prem private deployment, are there additional infra constraints? E.g., kernel versions, pinned NCCL?
[05:52] Diego: Yes. For private deployments we validate CUDA/cudNN/cuBLAS versions and kernel modules. Some optimized INT8/AWQ kernels require specific compiler flags and driver versions. We'll provide a checklist. Also driver mismatches can cause silent perf hits — important to align versions.
[06:10] Lena: Any security implications of storing KV cache in quantized form?
[06:15] Diego: The cache is still in-memory, and for private deployments you control the host. Quantized buffers don't change encryption at rest in our private control plane; KV cache isn't persisted to disk by default unless you enable long-term cache, which we recommend encrypting. For hosted, we have SOC2 controls and KMS integration. We'll send details.
[06:34] Omar: Back to accuracy numbers — did you say AWQ is often better than GPTQ? Can you share specific eval deltas?
[06:40] Diego: Sure — for a representative Llama-derivative 7B on our internal eval set: GPTQ produced +6.5% perplexity increase and 4.2% drop on instruction F1; AWQ produced +2.1% perplexity increase and 1.0% drop on instruction F1. But that's model and data dependent. We always recommend running benchmarks on your traced workload.
[07:05] Lena: Those are promising. What about FP8 results?
[07:09] Diego: FP8 on the same eval gave nearly identical quality to fp16 with slightly better memory; but again FP8 requires hardware+driver/kernel support. If you can standardize on A200 or newer with updated drivers, it may be worthwhile long-term.
[07:22] Maya: interjection, we had a client where hybrid AWQ+FP8 strategy gave the best unit economics — AWQ for most layers, FP8 for outlier-heavy layers.
[07:32] Omar: On model rollout, if we do AWQ in production and see regression in certain edge prompts, can Redwood route to fp16 fallback automatically?
[07:39] Diego: Yes, Redwood's smart routing can fallback per-request. You can set policy: if model_quality_score < threshold or user risk flag true, route to fp16 or a canary model. We also support canary rollouts at traffic % and automated regression detection via eval prompt sets.
[07:58] Priya: For running the benchmarks, what config should we use? Batch sizes? sequence length? tokenization?
[08:03] Diego: We'll share a benchmark template but quick suggestions: run 512 and 2048 context lengths, batch sizes 1, 8, 32 depending on latency vs throughput; measure tokens/s, p50/p95 token latency, memory consumption, and top-k/ppl metrics. Also include a mix of short interactive prompts and long generation traces to capture KV cache behavior.
[08:26] Omar: Are there known failure modes for AWQ on certain layers or attention patterns?
[08:30] Diego: AWQ struggles if a few neurons have extremely high dynamic range and if group size is too large — that dilutes precision for those outliers. We sometimes recommend smaller group sizes or keeping the attention/output projection layers in fp16.
[08:45] Lena: For 13B, do you recommend starting with AWQ or GPTQ?
[08:49] Diego: Start with AWQ if your priority is quality; start with GPTQ if you need a very fast pipeline and have the ability to iterate on calibration. For 13B, memory benefits are larger so mixed precision + AWQ is a common strategy.
[09:03] Omar: How long do quantization jobs take for our 7B? We have limited maintenance windows.
[09:08] Diego: Full GPTQ quant with good calibration on 7B might take 1-2 hours on a beefy GPU; AWQ passes are similar or slightly longer depending on group sizes. We can run offline and deliver artifacts. If you need faster, there's a quicker but less optimal path.
[09:22] Maya: Let's talk about the pilot plan — Redwood can run a pilot on a dedicated pool with metrics dashboards and eval alerts; typical pilot is 4-8 weeks. Pricing and pilot plan will be in the follow-up.
[09:33] Lena: Sounds good. Any examples of regression metrics we should monitor besides ppl and F1?
[09:38] Diego: Monitor semantic similarity scores, instruction-following pass rates, and hallucination rate on a curated prompt set. Also track per-user error spikes so you can rollback quickly.
[09:51] Omar: A couple of quick clarifying things: 1) if we keep KV cache quantized, does that require changes in our client integration? 2) does Redwood expose per-token cost breakdown with quantization flags?
[10:02] Diego: 1) No client changes—server-side only; if you use streaming tokens, same API. 2) Yes, Redwood Console will show token-level cost, model variant, and quantization profile applied per-route.
[10:14] Priya: One operational concern — we've had quiet perf regressions after driver updates. Can Redwood alert or detect such regression post-deploy?
[10:20] Diego: We have runtime tracing and can alert on baseline metric drift after infra changes; for private deployments we can run daily smoke checks and report.
[10:28] Maya: ok, quick recap and next steps: Redwood to run AWQ+GPTQ bench on 7B with 512 and 2048 contexts; share template and security/VPC docs; Cypher to provide traces and infra inventory. Schedule follow-up during week of 2027-04-11.
[10:45] Lena: Confirmed. Also we'll add a few edge-case prompts to the benchmark set.
[10:50] Omar: Thanks Diego, Maya.
[10:52] Maya: Thanks all. We'll send notes and action items.

(End of meeting - ~52min)
